```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::knit_hooks$set(small_mar = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before) par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(small_mar = TRUE)

library(bbmle)

occ <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_occupancy.csv")
counts <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")

# occupancy: the logistic decline, and a single p for every year
occ_nll2 <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(occ_nll2) <- c("a", "b")
occ_data <- list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied, n_routes = occ$n_routes,
                 elapsed = occ$elapsed)
m_occ <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2, start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05), data = occ_data)

const_nll <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes){
  p <- plogis(params[1])
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(const_nll) <- "a"
m_const <- mle2(minuslogl = const_nll, start = c(a = 1),
                data = list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied, n_routes = occ$n_routes))
dev_occ <- 2 * (m_const@min - m_occ@min)

# 2,000 nonsense predictors, fitted exactly with glm
base_glm <- glm(cbind(n_occupied, n_routes - n_occupied) ~ elapsed,
                data = occ, family = binomial)
set.seed(18)
junk_gain <- replicate(2000, {
  occ$junk <- rnorm(nrow(occ))
  (deviance(base_glm) - deviance(update(base_glm, . ~ . + junk))) / 2
})

# the guarded straight line from Lecture 16
lin_nll <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){
  p <- params[1] + params[2] * elapsed
  if (any(p <= 0 | p >= 1)) { return(1e6) }
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(lin_nll) <- c("a", "b")
m_lin <- mle2(minuslogl = lin_nll, start = c(a = 0.9, b = -0.008), data = occ_data)

# abundance: four models
m_flat  <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0, size = k),
                start = list(mu0 = 10, k = 1.4), data = counts)
m_year  <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(r * elapsed), size = k),
                start = list(mu0 = 15, r = -0.03, k = 1.4), data = counts)
m_urban <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(b * frac_built), size = k),
                start = list(mu0 = 12, b = -3, k = 1.4), data = counts)
m_both  <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(b * frac_built + r * elapsed),
                                size = k),
                start = list(mu0 = 15, b = -3, r = -0.03, k = 1.4), data = counts)
m_int   <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(b * frac_built + r * elapsed +
                                             i * frac_built * elapsed),
                                size = k),
                start = list(mu0 = 15, b = -3, r = -0.03, i = 0, k = 1.4),
                data = counts)

# the development model under three distributions, for the comparing-
# distributions slide (log scale, so no NaN warnings)
dist_po <- mle2(count ~ dpois(lambda = exp(log_mu0 + b * frac_built)),
                start = list(log_mu0 = 2.5, b = -3), data = counts)
dist_nb <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = exp(log_mu0 + b * frac_built),
                                size = exp(log_k)),
                start = list(log_mu0 = 2.5, b = -3, log_k = 0), data = counts)
dist_nm <- mle2(count ~ dnorm(mean = exp(log_mu0 + b * frac_built),
                              sd = exp(log_s)),
                start = list(log_mu0 = 2.5, b = -3, log_s = 2), data = counts)

# two species on one development gradient, zeros included
birds <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bbs_two_species.csv")
birds$species <- factor(birds$species, levels = c("cardinal", "bobwhite"))
bird_form <- count ~ dnbinom(mu = exp(log_mu0 + b * frac_built), size = exp(log_k))
bird_start <- list(log_mu0 = 2, b = 0, log_k = 0)
bird_fit <- function(pars){
  mle2(bird_form, start = bird_start, data = birds, parameters = pars)
}
m_same <- bird_fit(NULL)
m_mu   <- bird_fit(list(log_mu0 ~ species))
m_b    <- bird_fit(list(b ~ species))
m_mub  <- bird_fit(list(log_mu0 ~ species, b ~ species))
m_muk  <- bird_fit(list(log_mu0 ~ species, log_k ~ species))
m_all  <- bird_fit(list(log_mu0 ~ species, b ~ species, log_k ~ species))
cf_all <- coef(m_all)
bird_par <- data.frame(
  mu0 = exp(c(cf_all[["log_mu0.(Intercept)"]],
              cf_all[["log_mu0.(Intercept)"]] + cf_all[["log_mu0.speciesbobwhite"]])),
  b = c(cf_all[["b.(Intercept)"]],
        cf_all[["b.(Intercept)"]] + cf_all[["b.speciesbobwhite"]]),
  k = exp(c(cf_all[["log_k.(Intercept)"]],
            cf_all[["log_k.(Intercept)"]] + cf_all[["log_k.speciesbobwhite"]])),
  row.names = c("cardinal", "bobwhite"))
bird_par$halving <- 100 * log(2) / abs(bird_par$b)
p_b_after_mu <- anova(m_mu, m_mub)[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"]

aic_tab <- function(...){
  nms <- vapply(as.list(substitute(list(...)))[-1], deparse, character(1))
  tab <- AICtab(..., mnames = nms, base = TRUE, weights = TRUE)
  data.frame(model = attr(tab, "row.names"), AIC = round(tab$AIC, 1),
             dAIC = round(tab$dAIC, 1), parameters = tab$df,
             weight = ifelse(tab$weight < 0.001, "<0.001",
                             sprintf("%.3f", tab$weight)))
}
```

# Which model is better?

## The story so far {.smaller}

- **Lower NLL = better fit.** The best estimate is the bottom of the curve
- **Confidence interval** (Tuesday): every value within **1.92** of the bottom
- **Today:** the same idea for **whole models**, and AIC when that does not work

It takes a few minutes. **Once only**: from now on, `library(biometrydata)` is all
you need.

::: {.notes}
The download is the whole course repository, about 280 MB; it took 3.6 minutes
on a good connection when tested. With the whole room downloading at once it may
take longer, so this is a good moment to take questions on Assignment 3.

Two settings in that block exist to prevent the usual failures:

- options(timeout = 600): R's default download timeout is 60 seconds, which a
  280 MB download can exceed, and the install then fails with a confusing
  message about a connection.
- upgrade = "never": otherwise install_github may stop and ask whether to
  update a list of other packages, and students do not know what to answer.

If someone's install fails or stalls, they can keep going with the downloads
instead, which give identical data:

  occ <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bobwhite_occupancy.csv")
  counts <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")

and install at home.

Reinstalling the same way picks up any updates to the data.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(bbmle)
library(biometrydata)

occ <- bobwhite_occupancy       # straight from the package
counts <- bobwhite_counts

# Tuesday's occupancy model: the share of routes with bobwhite, falling with year
occ_nll2 <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(occ_nll2) <- c("a", "b")
occ_data <- list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied, n_routes = occ$n_routes,
                 elapsed = occ$elapsed)
m_occ <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2, start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05), data = occ_data)
m_occ@min
```
:::

**Check:** `r round(m_occ@min, 2)`, as on Tuesday.

## More parameters never fit worse {.smaller}

The single-$p$ model is the logistic model **with $b$ set to 0**.

So the optimizer fitting the logistic model could always just choose $b = 0$ and
match it. The extra parameter can only help.

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  model = c("one p for every year", "p changes with year"),
  parameters = c(1, 2),
  NLL = round(c(m_const@min, m_occ@min), 2)))
```

. . .

So a lower NLL alone proves nothing. **Would any extra parameter have done this
well?**

::: {.plain}
A model with an extra knob can always match the simpler model, so it always fits at least as well. Fitting better is not evidence on its own.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the problem the whole lecture solves, so make sure it lands before moving
on.

The logic is worth saying slowly: the bigger model contains the smaller one. At
worst the extra parameter sits at zero and changes nothing; at best it soaks up
something. It can never make the fit worse, which means "it fit better" is true of
every extra parameter ever added, including ones that mean nothing.
:::

## Even nonsense helps {.smaller}

Add a column of **random numbers** as a second predictor. Do it 2,000 times:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-width: 7.4
hist(junk_gain, breaks = seq(0, ceiling(max(junk_gain) * 4) / 4, by = 0.125),
     col = "grey75", border = "white", main = "",
     xlab = "improvement in NLL from a column of random numbers",
     ylab = "number of tries")
abline(v = qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#762a83")
text(qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2, par("usr")[4] * 0.85, "1.92", pos = 4,
     col = "#762a83")
```

**Every one** improved the fit. A median of
`r round(median(junk_gain), 2)`, and `r round(100 * mean(junk_gain > 1.92), 0)`%
by more than 1.92.

::: {.notes}
The picture to remember. All 2,000 bars sit to the right of zero: not one random
column made the fit worse, because none of them can.

The 1.92 line is Tuesday's threshold. Almost all nonsense falls short of it,
which is exactly what the threshold is for: an improvement bigger than 1.92 is
bigger than what random numbers usually manage.

If anyone asks why only 2% cross it rather than 5%: these particular occupancy
data scatter a little less than a binomial predicts, so random predictors find
even less to latch onto. With a typical dataset it would be close to 5%. Not
worth more than a sentence.

The same experiment is in the old version of this lecture with R-squared and lm.
It gives the same lesson: fit always improves.
:::

## Try it: a nonsense predictor {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
junk <- runif(nrow(occ))      # 23 random numbers: related to nothing

occ_junk <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed, junk){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed + params[3] * junk)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(occ_junk) <- c("a", "b", "c")

m_junk <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_junk,
               start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05, c = 0),
               data = c(occ_data, list(junk = junk)))

m_occ@min - m_junk@min        # how much did nonsense "improve" the fit?
```
:::

**Compare with your neighbor.** Everyone has different random numbers.

::: {.notes}
Everyone gets a positive number, and almost everyone gets a small one. Ask for a
show of hands: who got more than 1? More than 1.92? There may be one in the
room.

The point of doing it rather than only seeing the histogram: they made the
nonsense themselves, so there is no doubt that the improvement means nothing.

c(occ_data, list(junk = junk)) adds the new column to the list of data mle2
already has. Mention it only if asked.
:::

# The likelihood ratio test

## Nested models {.smaller}

Start with the biggest model. Each one below it is **nested** in it:

| Model | Equation | Fix in the biggest | Number fixed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Biggest | $Y = m_1 X_1 + m_2 X_2 + b$ | | |
| Smaller | $Y = m_1 X_1 + b$ | $m_2 = 0$ | 1 |
| Smallest | $Y = b$ | $m_1 = m_2 = 0$ | 2 |
| Equal slopes | $Y = m (X_1 + X_2) + b$ | $m_1 = m_2$ | 1 |

. . .

**Not nested:** $Y = m_1 X_1 + b$ against $Y = m_2 X_2 + b$, or $Y = m X + b$
against $Y = b\,e^{mX}$

::: {.plain}
Nested: you get the smaller model by setting the bigger one's parameters to zero, or equal to each other. Keep count of how many you fix: the test on the next slide needs it.
:::

::: {.notes}
The definition, in symbols. Say it in words too: nested means you can get the
smaller model by switching off a piece of the bigger one. Year against
development, in the bobwhite counts, is the instructive "not nested" case: same
number of parameters, and neither is the other with a piece switched off.

Map it onto today's bobwhite counts: on the log scale, the "both" model is
log(mu) = r * year + b * development + log(mu0). Set the development slope to
zero and you have the year model; set both to zero and you have the flat model.
That is rows 1 to 3 of the table.

Why the two "not nested" pairs fail: in the first, neither is the other with a
piece switched off; in the second, the shapes differ, so no parameter value turns
one into the other.

The "equal slopes" row is worth a moment because it is not obvious that it
counts as nested: nothing is set to zero, but two parameters are forced to be
the same, which removes one. It is exactly the question in Assignment 3, Part 1a:
is a female of the other species as harmful as one of your own (a12 = a11)?

The last column becomes the degrees of freedom for the likelihood ratio test on
the next slide, which is where the term is introduced. Do not use it here.
:::

## The test {.smaller}

Same as Tuesday, pointed at two models:

$$\text{deviance} = 2 \times \big(\text{NLL}_{\text{smaller}} - \text{NLL}_{\text{bigger}}\big)$$

If the smaller model is true, the deviance follows a **chi-squared**
distribution. Its one setting, the **degrees of freedom**, is here simply **the
number of parameters you fixed**: the last column of the previous slide.

. . .

| Extra parameters | The bigger model must improve the NLL by more than |
|---|---|
| 1 | **1.92** |
| 2 | 3.00 |
| 3 | 3.91 |


::: {.plain}
If the extra parameters were useless, an improvement this big would be rare. So when we see one, we keep them.
:::

::: {.notes}
On Tuesday every interval used the first row: one parameter fixed at a time.

The table is qchisq(0.95, df) / 2 for df = 1, 2, 3. It is worth seeing that the
bar per parameter falls as you add more at once: three parameters need 3.91,
not 3 times 1.92. Not worth dwelling on.

Same caveat as Tuesday: this is an approximation that is good with reasonable
amounts of data, and the book is honest about that.
:::

## By hand, then with `anova()` {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
const_nll <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes){
  p <- plogis(params[1])                      # no year: one p for every year
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(const_nll) <- "a"
m_const <- mle2(minuslogl = const_nll, start = c(a = 1),
                data = list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied, n_routes = occ$n_routes))

deviance_occ <- 2 * (m_const@min - m_occ@min)
deviance_occ
pchisq(deviance_occ, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)   # the p-value

anova(m_const, m_occ)                              # the same test, in one line
```
:::

**Check:** a deviance of `r round(dev_occ, 1)`. R prints the p-value as
`9.439462e-12`, which means 0.0000000000094: the e-12 moves the decimal point 12 places left.

::: {.notes}
Lecture 16 promised this: the trend model beat the one-number model by 23 units,
twice that is 46, and against a threshold of 3.84 it is not close.

pchisq with lower.tail = FALSE gives the probability of a deviance at least this
large if the smaller model were true. That is a p-value in the usual sense.

anova() on two mle2 fits runs exactly this test, and the next slide reads its
output.
:::

## Reading `anova()` {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
anova(m_const, m_occ)
```

- `Deviance` is $2 \times$ NLL for each model
- `Chisq` is the **difference**: the test statistic
- `Df` is how many parameters were fixed to get the smaller model
- `Pr(>Chisq)` is the p-value

::: {.plain}
A small p-value means the bigger model gained more than chance would give it. Keep the bigger model.
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the table left to right once. The column called Deviance is twice the NLL,
which confuses people because it is not the deviance from the formula two slides
ago; that one is in the Chisq column.

Do not interpret the result yet; the next slide does, so that reading the table
and drawing the conclusion are separate steps.
:::

## So which model wins? {.smaller}

| | NLL | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| one $p$ for every year | `r round(m_const@min, 1)` | 1 |
| $p$ changes with year | `r round(m_occ@min, 1)` | 2 |

. . .

- The year model improves the NLL by **`r round(m_const@min - m_occ@min, 1)`**.
  Chance alone would rarely give more than **1.92**
- The p-value is far below 0.05: about **`r round(pchisq(dev_occ, 1, lower.tail = FALSE) * 1e12)` in a trillion**

. . .

**The year model wins.** Bobwhite occupancy really is declining; a flat line
does not fit the data.

::: {.notes}
The conclusion stated outright, because the previous slide only taught how to
read the table.

Connect it to Tuesday: the confidence interval for b excluded zero, and this is
the same finding reached as a test. Two routes, one answer, which is the point of
the "which tool, when" slide at the end.
:::

## Your turn: test the nonsense {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Earlier you added a column of random numbers to the model. Test it the same way:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
anova(m_occ, m_junk)
```
:::

**Is the p-value above or below 0.05? Which model do you keep?**

. . .

It should be **well above 0.05**: the random column did not gain more than
chance would. **Keep the simpler model**, `m_occ`.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Here the smaller model is m_occ and the bigger one is m_junk, the
reverse of the order on the previous slides only in which names are which.

Anyone whose random numbers gave p below 0.05 is the one in twenty the test is
designed to let through, and it is worth congratulating them for it: it is the
5% in "5% level", happening in front of them.
:::

# AIC

## When models are not nested {.smaller}

Last Thursday: do bobwhite counts follow **year** or **development**? Same number
of parameters, neither a special case of the other. **No likelihood ratio test.**

. . .

$$\text{AIC} = 2 \times \text{NLL} + 2 \times (\text{number of parameters})$$

- **Lower is better**, as with the NLL
- Each parameter costs **1 unit** of NLL. Compare: the test's 1.92
- Only **differences** mean anything. An AIC of 9079 on its own says nothing

. . .

Works for **any** set of models fitted to **the same data**.

::: {.plain}
AIC is how badly a model fits, plus a charge for every parameter. The lowest total wins.
:::

::: {.notes}
Akaike's information criterion. The formula is short enough to compute by hand,
and they should do it once so it is not a black box.

Where the penalty comes from, in one sentence for anyone who asks: a model's fit
to its own data is optimistic, because it was tuned to that data; AIC estimates
how well the model would do on new data from the same process, and the
optimism works out to about one NLL unit per parameter. That is the reason for
the 2 in 2k.

The penalty is gentler than the test's 1.92, so AIC is a little more willing to
keep a parameter. That is by design: AIC is aimed at prediction, the test at
deciding whether an effect is there at all.
:::

## A shortcut: the formula version {.smaller}

Every model so far was a function, then `mle2()`. For a one-line model there is
a shortcut: **write the model as a formula**.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Function**

```{r}
#| eval: false
urban_nll2 <- function(params, y, u){
  mu <- params[1] * exp(params[2] * u)
  -sum(dnbinom(y, mu = mu,
               size = params[3],
               log = TRUE))
}
parnames(urban_nll2) <- c("mu0", "b", "k")
mle2(minuslogl = urban_nll2,
     start = c(mu0 = 12, b = -3, k = 1.4),
     data = list(y = counts$count,
                 u = counts$frac_built))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Formula**

```{r}
#| eval: false
mle2(count ~ dnbinom(
       mu = mu0 * exp(b * frac_built),
       size = k),
     start = list(mu0 = 12, b = -3,
                  k = 1.4),
     data = counts)
```

Read it as: *count is negative binomial, with this mean and this size.*
:::

::::

**Same model, same answer.** The formula version is what the assignment uses.

::: {.notes}
Worth five minutes, because the whole starter script is written this way and
it looks like a different language until someone points out it is the same model.

How to read it: left of the tilde is the data column; right of it is the
distribution, written as its d function without the x and without log = TRUE.
mle2 fills those in, takes the negative log-likelihood, and sums it. Column names
in the formula are looked up in the data frame; anything not in the data frame
is treated as a parameter, and must be in start.

The function version still matters. A model with an if statement, a loop, or a
guard like Lecture 16's straight line cannot be written as a formula.
:::

## Three models for the counts {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
m_flat <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0, size = k),
               start = list(mu0 = 10, k = 1.4), data = counts)

m_year <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(r * elapsed), size = k),
               start = list(mu0 = 15, r = -0.03, k = 1.4), data = counts)

m_urban <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(b * frac_built), size = k),
                start = list(mu0 = 12, b = -3, k = 1.4), data = counts)

AIC(m_flat)
2 * m_flat@min + 2 * 2     # the same number, by hand
```
:::

$$\text{AIC} = 2 \times \text{NLL} + 2 \times (\text{number of parameters})$$

By hand: `m_flat@min` is the NLL, and `m_flat` has **2** parameters, `mu0` and
`k`. **Check:** both lines give `r round(AIC(m_flat), 1)`.

::: {.notes}
m_year uses an exponential decline, mu0 * exp(r * elapsed), rather than the
(1 - decline)^year of Lectures 15 and 16. They are the same curve written two ways: r is
log(1 - decline). Mention it only if someone notices.

The by-hand line is there so that AIC is arithmetic they have done, not a number
R produced. Two parameters, so the penalty is 4.

Expect NaN warnings while fitting: the optimizer tries a negative k or mu0 on
its way to the answer. They are harmless here, and the fits converge.
:::

## Your turn: year **and** development {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Does a model with **both** do better than either alone?

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
m_both <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(b * frac_built + r * elapsed),
                               size = k),
               start = list(mu0 = 15, b = -3, r = -0.03, k = 1.4),
               data = counts)

# compare all four with AICtab(). Give it the four fitted models, and
# base = TRUE so it shows the AIC itself and not only the differences
```
:::

. . .

Which is best? **Is year versus development a question the likelihood ratio test
could have answered?**

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. The answer is

  AICtab(m_flat, m_year, m_urban, m_both, base = TRUE)

The second question is the check on the nested slide: no, year and development
are not nested in each other, so only AIC can rank them. Each is nested in
m_both, though, so a test could ask whether adding the other one helps.
:::

## Reading `AICtab()` {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(aic_tab(m_flat, m_year, m_urban, m_both), row.names = FALSE)
```

- `dAIC`: how far behind the best model. **0 is the best**
- Rough guide: under **2**, about as good; over **10**, essentially no support
- `weight`: the share of support among **these** models

. . .

**Both matter**, and development more than year. Neither replaces the other:
development explains **where** bobwhite are scarce, year **how fast** they are
going.

::: {.notes}
The guide is Burnham and Anderson's, and it is a convention rather than a law.
Students will want a hard threshold; the honest answer is that a dAIC of 3 is a
judgment call and 75 is not.

Weights are worth one caution: they are shares among the models you happened to
fit. A weight of 1 means "best of these four", not "true". Add a fifth model and
every weight changes.

The biological reading closes the loop from Lecture 16, which said the two
covariates answered different questions because development does not change over
time. The comparison says both are needed, which is the same conclusion arrived at
by a number.

If anyone computes it: development alone beats year alone by about 43 AIC units.
:::

## What AIC cannot see {.smaller}

Lecture 16's two occupancy curves, both with two parameters:

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(aic_tab(m_lin, m_occ), row.names = FALSE)
```

`m_lin` is the guarded straight line. AIC prefers it.

. . .

It also predicts an occupancy **below zero** by 2100.

. . .

**AIC ranks only the models you give it, and only on fit.** Whether a model is
biologically possible is your job.

::: {.notes}
A deliberate callback. Lecture 16 rejected the straight line on biology, and AIC
cannot know that: it sees two models with the same number of parameters and
picks the one with the lower NLL.

A dAIC of 2.2 is in the "about as good" zone anyway, so the honest summary is
that the data cannot tell these shapes apart and biology breaks the tie.

The general lesson for the assignment: AIC chooses among candidates. Choosing the
candidates is the scientific part, and it is the part they will be graded on in
Part 2.
:::

# Do two species differ?

## Two birds, one gradient {.smaller}

**Northern Cardinal**: feeders, hedges, shrubby edges. **Northern Bobwhite**:
grassland and open pine. Every Florida route surveyed in 2019:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-width: 8.4
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.4, 3.6, 1.8, 0.6), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0))
uu <- seq(0, max(birds$frac_built), length.out = 200)
cols <- c(cardinal = "#b2182b", bobwhite = "#8c6d31")
for (sp in c("cardinal", "bobwhite")) {
  d <- birds[birds$species == sp, ]
  plot(d$frac_built, d$count, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(cols[sp], 0.55),
       xlab = "fraction developed", ylab = "birds counted", bty = "l")
  lines(uu, bird_par[sp, "mu0"] * exp(bird_par[sp, "b"] * uu), lwd = 3,
        col = cols[sp])
  mtext(sp, side = 3, line = 0.4, cex = 1.1)
}
```

**Does development affect them differently?**

::: {.notes}
The reading answers the same kind of question with balsam fir in two kinds of
stand. This is the same idea with birds the class already knows, on the same
development gradient as the abundance models earlier today.

One change from the earlier bobwhite counts: this table has the zeros. Every
route surveyed in 2019 has a row for each species, and a route where a species
was not recorded gets a 0. Bobwhite were missing from 19 of the 71 routes;
cardinals were on every one. The earlier counts file had no zeros, which the
BBS README warns about; data/class_examples/make_class_examples.R shows how they
were put back.

The curves are from the best model, which they will find themselves. Do not
give it away: the question is how the species differ, and there are three
possible answers.

Note the y axes differ: cardinals are counted in the tens to hundreds, bobwhite
in single figures.
:::

## Get set up, again {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
birds <- bbs_two_species          # from the course data package

head(birds)
table(birds$species)

# make cardinal the first level, so it is the baseline in the models
birds$species <- factor(birds$species, levels = c("cardinal", "bobwhite"))
```
:::

The development model from earlier, on the log scale to keep $\mu_0$ and $k$
positive:

$$\mu = \mu_0 \, e^{\,b \cdot \text{development}} \qquad \text{count} \sim \text{NegBin}(\mu, k)$$

**Three ways the species could differ:** in $\mu_0$ (birds where nothing is
built), in $b$ (how fast counts fall with development), or in $k$ (how variable
routes are).

::: {.notes}
142 rows: 71 routes, two species.

Anyone without the package:
birds <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bbs_two_species.csv")

Why the log scale: on the earlier count models a negative mu0 or k during the
search produced NaN warnings. Fitting log_mu0 and log_k makes every value legal,
which is the "keeping parameters legal" table from Lecture 16. exp() turns them
back.

k is the third way to differ and the one students forget: two species can have
the same average curve and still differ in how scattered routes are around it.
:::

## Letting a parameter differ: `parameters =` {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
form <- count ~ dnbinom(mu = exp(log_mu0 + b * frac_built), size = exp(log_k))
start <- list(log_mu0 = 2, b = 0, log_k = 0)

m_same <- mle2(form, start = start, data = birds)    # one model for both species

m_mu <- mle2(form, start = start, data = birds,
             parameters = list(log_mu0 ~ species))   # a separate mu0 for each

coef(m_mu)
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
round(coef(m_mu), 3)
```

`log_mu0.(Intercept)` is the **cardinal** value. `log_mu0.speciesbobwhite` is
**how much bobwhite differ** from it.

::: {.notes}
Saving the formula and the start list once saves typing them for every model,
since only the parameters line changes from here on.

parameters = list(log_mu0 ~ species) reads "log_mu0 depends on species". mle2
builds a baseline for the first level of species, cardinal, and a difference for
the other.

So the bobwhite value is the sum, about 4.0 + (-1.9) = 2.1 on the log scale. Make
them do the addition and then exp() once: exp(4.0) is about 54 cardinals where
nothing is built, exp(2.1) about 8 bobwhite. Reading speciesbobwhite as the
bobwhite value itself is the mistake everyone makes.

This is exactly what model 1b in the assignment does, letting int, b and the
scatter differ among resident, partial and full migrants.
:::

## Your turn: the other ways to differ {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
m_b <- mle2(form, start = start, data = birds,
            parameters = list(b ~ species))

# now fit three more, changing only the parameters line:
#   m_mub   log_mu0 and b both differ
#   m_muk   log_mu0 and log_k differ
#   m_all   all three differ

# then compare all six with AICtab(), base = TRUE
```
:::

**Which way do the species differ?**

::: {.notes}
Ten minutes. Each model is the same line with a different parameters list, for
example parameters = list(log_mu0 ~ species, b ~ species, log_k ~ species).

The common slip is forgetting to add the new model to the AICtab call.

These fits produce no warnings, thanks to the log scale.
:::

## Ranking the six models {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(aic_tab(m_same, m_mu, m_b, m_mub, m_muk, m_all), row.names = FALSE)
```

. . .

**`m_all`: all three differ**, with 90% of the weight.

::: {.notes}
Read the table from the bottom: one model for both species is far behind, as
expected for two birds this different. The best model lets all three differ.

Ask before the next slide: which do they think differs most? The next slide
answers it in numbers.
:::

## How they differ {.smaller}

| From `m_all` | cardinal | bobwhite |
|---|---|---|
| birds where nothing is built | `r round(bird_par["cardinal", "mu0"])` | `r round(bird_par["bobwhite", "mu0"])` |
| development that halves the count | `r round(bird_par["cardinal", "halving"])`% | `r round(bird_par["bobwhite", "halving"])`% |
| $k$: smaller means more variable | `r round(bird_par["cardinal", "k"], 2)` | `r round(bird_par["bobwhite", "k"], 2)` |

. . .

- Bobwhite lose birds to development **four times as fast**
- Bobwhite are far **patchier**: plentiful on some routes, absent from 19 of 71

::: {.plain}
Groups can differ in more than their average. Here the two species also differ in how fast development hurts them, and in how evenly they are spread.
:::

::: {.notes}
The halving numbers are log(2) / |b|, as in Lecture 16, now with an answer for
each species.

The patchiness is the interesting part and has a habitat explanation: bobwhite
need open grassland, old fields and fire-maintained pine, which are scattered
across Florida, so some routes have plenty and 19 have none. Cardinals use almost
any shrubby edge, including suburbs, so every route has them. The data say the
variability differs; habitat is the likely reason, not something these models
test.

The general lesson, and it matters for Part 2: if they only ever let the mean
differ between groups, they would miss two of the three differences here.
:::

## The test asks a narrower question {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
anova(m_same, m_mu, m_mub)
```

Adding a separate $\mu_0$: a huge gain. Adding $b$ **after** it: $p$ =
`r round(p_b_after_mu, 3)`.

. . .

A sequence of tests checks **one path** through the models, in the order you list
them. AIC compares **all of them at once**, and found the difference in $k$,
which this path never tried.

::: {.plain}
A test compares two models at a time. AIC lines up all of them at once.
:::

::: {.notes}
anova() with three models runs two tests: same against mu, then mu against mub.
Each line is a test of the model above it.

Worth being honest that this sequence would have stopped at m_mub, a model AIC
puts about 19 units behind the best. Nothing is wrong with the test; it answered
the question it was asked. The path just never visited k.

For the assignment: either approach is acceptable, but they should say which
they used and why. AIC is the one the assignment asks for.
:::

## Rules for a fair comparison {.smaller}

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| **Same rows** in every model | NLL adds up over rows; drop one and the NLL changes for reasons unrelated to the model. Run `na.omit()` on the data **once**, before fitting anything |
| **Same response**, on the same scale | `count` and `log(count)` have likelihoods on different scales. Never compare them by AIC |
| **Count every parameter**, including `k` and `sd` | AIC does it for you with `mle2`. By hand, people forget them |
| **Every model has to make sense** | AIC ranks only what you give it |

::: {.notes}
The first rule is the one that will bite in the assignment. The trap is
filtering the data differently for different models, for example running
na.omit() on only the columns each model uses. A model fitted to fewer rows has a
lower NLL simply because it is adding up fewer terms, and AIC will happily
crown it. The hawk model in the starter script runs na.omit() once, up front,
for this reason; they should keep that when they build alternatives.

The second rule catches people who log the response to make it look normal, fit
that, and compare it by AIC with a model of the raw response. The fix is to keep
the response the same and change the distribution, for example a lognormal on
the raw values, which is what model 1b does with wing length.

mle2 counts parameters correctly, including those created by parameters = ...:
m_all has six.
:::

## Comparing distributions {.smaller}

The bobwhite development model from earlier, with three different distributions:

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  distribution = c("negative binomial", "Poisson", "normal"),
  parameters = c(3, 2, 3),
  AIC = round(c(AIC(dist_nb), AIC(dist_po), AIC(dist_nm)), 1)))
```

. . .

- The negative binomial wins by about **`r round((AIC(dist_po) - AIC(dist_nb)) / 1000)`,000** units
- Both count models find the **same curve**: $b$ = `r round(coef(dist_nb)["b"], 1)` and
  `r round(coef(dist_po)["b"], 1)`. The distribution changes the fit, not the curve

. . .

The normal looks better than the Poisson. **That comparison is not allowed.**
Next slide.

::: {.notes}
The 7,000 units are Lecture 15's variance check turned into a number: the counts
are far more variable than a Poisson allows, and the negative binomial's extra
parameter, k, is worth it many times over.

The third row is the trap, deliberately left in. R computes an AIC for a normal
model of these counts without complaint, and it appears to beat the Poisson. Let
the room notice that before explaining why it is meaningless.
:::

## Rules for comparing distributions {.smaller}

- **Discrete with discrete, continuous with continuous.** A count model gives
  the **probability** of each count; a normal gives a **density**. Their AICs are
  in different units, so the normal row on the last slide cannot be compared
- **Same response, same scale.** For a measurement, try `dlnorm(y)` against
  `dgamma(y)`, never `dnorm(log(y))` against `dgamma(y)`
- **Count the distribution's own parameter**: $k$ for the negative binomial,
  the standard deviation for the normal
- **Poisson against negative binomial: use AIC**, not the likelihood ratio test

::: {.plain}
You can let AIC choose the distribution, as long as every candidate describes the same numbers in the same way: all counts, or all measurements.
:::

::: {.notes}
On the first rule: a Poisson probability is a number between 0 and 1. A normal
density depends on the units of measurement and can exceed 1, so its
log-likelihood can be shifted just by measuring in different units. Different
currencies; no exchange rate.

The second rule is the previous slide's "same response, same scale", applied to
distributions. dnorm on log(y) is a likelihood for a different response.

Why not the test for Poisson against negative binomial: the Poisson is the
negative binomial with k at infinity, the edge of what k can be, and the
chi-squared approximation breaks down at an edge. AIC has no such problem.

For the assignment: Part 1c starts as a Poisson on reef richness, and this slide
is the licence to change it.
:::

## Assignment 3, Part 1: a strategy {.smaller}

1. **Run the starter model** as given. Note its AIC.
2. **Remove one piece at a time**: a covariate, an exponent, a group effect.
   Fit each as its own model.
3. **`AICtab()`** them all together.
4. **Keep removing** from the best one until nothing improves.
5. **Write it down**: which model, and why, in a sentence of biology.

. . .

**Check the distribution before the terms.** If the data are far more variable
than the distribution allows, removing terms will not fix it.

::: {.notes}
A recipe, since "simplify an over-fit model" is open-ended enough to stall people.

The last line is a hint for model 1c, which starts as a Poisson on reef
richness whose variance is 4.4 times its mean. Switching to a negative binomial
improves AIC by more than 13,000 units, which dwarfs every other choice in that
model. A student who checks var / mean first, as in Lecture 15, has understood
the assignment.

Step 2 can include changing the shape, not only deleting: 1a invites a Ricker
model, which is not nested in the starting model and can only be compared by
AIC.

Removing one piece at a time is backward stepwise selection, which has known
problems in the statistics literature. For a teaching exercise with a handful of
candidates it is fine; if anyone asks, say so.
:::

## Which tool, when {.smaller}

| You want to know | Use | In plain words |
|---|---|---|
| Could this parameter be zero? | its **confidence interval**, `confint()` | is zero among the values the data cannot rule out? |
| Is the bigger of two **nested** models better? | **likelihood ratio test**, `anova()` | did the extra parameters gain more than chance would? |
| Which of **several** models is best? | **AIC**, `AICtab()` | lowest fit-plus-charge wins; within 2 is a tie |
| Does the model make biological sense? | **you** | no statistic checks this |

::: {.notes}
The recap slide for today, and the one to photograph for the assignment. It
replaces a separate "what you can now do" list.

The first row is Tuesday, the next two are today. Point out that rows 1 and 2
are the same question asked two ways: "is b different from zero" and "is the
model with b better than the model without it" give the same answer.

The last row is the one people forget, and it is the one that Part 2 of the
assignment is graded on most.
:::

## Additional practice {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Is development **worse for bobwhite in later years**? Let the effect of
development change with year:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# 1. add a term i * frac_built * elapsed inside exp(), next to the other two,
#    and an i = 0 in start. Call the model m_int
# 2. is m_both nested in m_int? Then compare them with anova()
# 3. and with AICtab(). Do the test and AIC agree?
# 4. which would you report, and why?
```
:::

::: {.notes}
For outside class, or for anyone who finishes early.

Answers: i = -0.069, LRT p = 0.14, dAIC 0.2 in favor of m_int. So the test says
the interaction is not supported and AIC calls it a tie. They do not really
disagree: a dAIC under 2 means the data cannot tell the models apart, and with a
tie the simpler model is the one to report.

That is a useful thing to have seen once before Part 2, where it will happen.
:::
